summary: Specifies attribute types and object classes for LDAP directory clients, for services such as white pages. They are widely used as the basis for schemas in many directories. It does not cover server administration. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A ready-made set of form fields for people-directory entries, such as name, phone and email.

subtitle: The standard set of attribute types and object classes for people, organizations and groups in LDAP directories.

tldr.problem: LDAP clients building directory services such as white pages need agreed names and definitions for common data like names, addresses, phone numbers and groups.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines 43 attribute types and 14 object classes, each with an OID, a syntax and matching rules, most taken from the X.500 documents.
tldr.outcome: These definitions are widely used as the basis for the schema in many LDAP directories. RFC 4519 obsoletes RFC 2256 and is the definitive description for use in LDAP.

today: RFC 4519 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 2256. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope and Relationship to Other Specs
sections.content:
This document gives attribute types and object classes for LDAP directory clients, for services such as White Pages. They were originally specified in the X.500 documents. The RFC does not cover attributes used to administer directory servers, nor objects defined for specific uses in other documents.

It is part of the LDAP technical specification (RFC 4510). It obsoletes RFC 2256: Sections 6 and 8 of that RFC moved to RFC 4517, Sections 5.1, 5.2, 7.1 and 7.2 moved to RFC 4512, and the rest is replaced here. It supersedes the dc attribute type and dcObject class from RFC 2247, and updates RFC 2798 (the uid attribute) and RFC 2377 (the uidObject class). PKI-related schema moved to RFC 4523. The descriptions here SHALL be considered definitive for use in LDAP.
sections.eli5: This is the official list of standard fields for a directory. It replaces an older list and hands a few topics to other documents.

sections.title: Attribute Types
sections.content:
Section 2 describes 43 attribute types that hold user information. Each entry gives a description, whether values are multi-valued, its source (mostly X.520), a formal definition with an OID, and examples. Definitions are written in the ABNF of AttributeTypeDescription from RFC 4512.

Servers SHOULD recognize all of them except searchGuide and teletexTerminalIdentifier, which servers need not implement and whose use is greatly discouraged. Typical examples: cn holds names of an object, sn a family name, c a two-letter ISO 3166 country code, telephoneNumber numbers following ITU E.123, and postalAddress postal addresses.

Several types are supertypes. name is the supertype of naming attributes such as cn, sn, o, ou, l, st and title. distinguishedName is the base for DN-valued attributes such as member, owner, roleOccupant and seeAlso. Clients MUST NOT assume servers support attribute subtyping.

The dc attribute holds one label of a DNS name, so example is valid but example.com is not. The directory does not enforce the label rules; the client must. Applications supporting internationalized domain names SHALL use the ToASCII method from RFC 3490.
sections.eli5: Each attribute is one labelled box on a form, like Name, City or Phone, and the RFC says what may go in each box.

sections.title: Object Classes
sections.content:
Section 3 defines 14 object classes. An object class says what kind of thing an entry represents, which attributes it MUST have and which it MAY have. Servers SHOULD recognize all of them as values of objectClass.

Most are structural and descend from top. Examples are person (MUST have sn and cn), organizationalPerson (a person in relation to an organization), organization (MUST have o), organizationalUnit (MUST have ou), organizationalRole, residentialPerson, country, locality, device and applicationProcess.

For groups there are groupOfNames and groupOfUniqueNames. Both must have cn and a member attribute (member or uniqueMember). The unique version is for when object names are not repeated or reassigned within a set scope.

dcObject and uidObject are auxiliary, meaning they are added alongside an existing structural class to carry dc or uid.
sections.eli5: An object class is the type of form. A Person form has to have a name filled in, while an Organization form has to have the organization's name.

sections.title: Passwords and Privacy
sections.content:
Attributes describe real-world people, organizations and devices, and most countries have privacy laws about publishing information on people.

The userPassword attribute holds octet strings. Textual passwords SHOULD be transcoded to Unicode, prepared with SASLprep (RFC 4013) and encoded as UTF-8. Passwords are not encrypted by the syntax, and sending cleartext passwords is strongly discouraged where the transport cannot guarantee confidentiality and integrity.

Multiple userPassword values need care. The RFC says one case is two passwords for consecutive periods, but resetting a password without knowing the old one gets tricky or impossible when several values are present. Applications that replace values should use modify/replaceValues, and servers are encouraged to offer a control that limits the attribute to one value. For authentication, the user need only prove knowledge of one value.
sections.eli5: Passwords should never be sent in the open, and having several passwords stored for one person can cause trouble when you need to reset them.

sections.title: IANA Registry Updates
sections.content:
IANA updated the LDAP descriptors registry so that the short names defined here point to RFC 4519. The table lists each name, whether it is an attribute (A) or object class (O), and its OID. Alternate names such as commonName, countryName, domainComponent, surname and userid are included.

Names that need to be reserved rather than assigned, such as gn, carry the value RESERVED in place of an OID. The author and change controller for these entries is the IESG.
sections.eli5: The official list of field names was updated so that each name points back to this document.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2256
sections.content:
The appendix lists 28 changes. Main ones: syntaxes and matching rules were removed because they moved to RFC 4517, and certificate-related attribute types and classes (such as userCertificate and certificationAuthority) were removed in favour of RFC 4523. The dmdName, knowledgeInformation and presentationAddress attribute types and the dmd, applicationEntity and dSA classes were removed too. Section 1.1 says that elements not carried forward are to be considered Historic unless reintroduced.

New material includes Security and IANA sections, an explanation and example for each element, the dc attribute with its stored and query rules for internationalized names, the dcObject and uidObject definitions, and the SASLprep text for userPassword.
sections.eli5: This lists what was moved, removed or added compared with the older version.
